CausalChain: NAFLD-induced metabolic stress -> Upregulation of FTO in hepatocytes -> FTO-mediated m6A demethylation on select lipid metabolism gene mRNAs -> Enhanced mRNA stability and translation -> Accumulation of lipotoxic metabolites -> Amplification via ROS and α-dicarbonyl stress -> Activation of inflammatory and parallel RNF5/RAGE signaling pathways -> Recruitment of immunosuppressive cells (Tregs, MDSCs) -> Formation of a pro-tumorigenic microenvironment -> Progression to hepatocellular carcinoma
Hypothesis: In liver cells under NAFLD-induced metabolic stress, there is a coordinated upregulation of FTO which specifically demethylates m6A marks on mRNAs encoding pivotal lipid metabolic enzymes. The resultant mRNA stabilization and increased translation elevate the production of these enzymes, driving the accumulation of lipotoxic metabolites. This metabolic imbalance is further exacerbated by concurrent ROS and carbonyl stress, which potentiate alternative inflammatory pathways such as the RNF5/IGF2BP1 axis and RAGE signaling. Together, these mechanisms induce a robust inflammatory response and recruit immunosuppressive cells, thereby establishing a microenvironment that favors the progression from NAFLD to hepatocellular carcinoma. The use of state-of-the-art omics techniques (e.g., single-cell RNA-seq, m6A-RIP-seq, and spatial profiling) will enable the identification of FTO’s precise mRNA targets and the dissection of this complex regulatory network, providing novel therapeutic targets.
Abstract: We propose that in non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), metabolic stress exerts a dual influence by upregulating the RNA demethylase FTO and concurrently activating complementary metabolic stress pathways, such as reactive oxygen species (ROS) and carbonyl stress. FTO selectively demethylates N6-methyladenosine (m6A) modifications on a specific subset of mRNAs encoding key lipid metabolic enzymes, thereby increasing their stability and translation. This heightened enzyme activity leads to a controlled but deleterious accumulation of lipotoxic metabolites, which in turn amplify inflammatory signals and synergize with ROS‐ and α-dicarbonyl-mediated stress to upregulate parallel immune-modulatory axes (e.g., RNF5/IGF2BP1 and RAGE pathways). The convergence of these signaling cascades facilitates the recruitment of immunosuppressive cell populations, such as regulatory T cells (Tregs) and myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), ultimately establishing a pro-tumorigenic microenvironment that promotes the progression from NAFLD to hepatocellular carcinoma. Leveraging contemporary high-throughput and single-cell omics technologies—including RNA-seq, m6A-RIP-seq, and digital spatial profiling—this hypothesis not only refines the mechanistic understanding but also provides actionable insights for experimental validation and therapeutic intervention.
Orignal_vs_New: The revised hypothesis retains the original causal chain by proposing that NAFLD-induced metabolic stress leads to FTO upregulation, m6A demethylation of lipid metabolic gene mRNAs, mRNA stabilization, lipotoxic metabolite accumulation, inflammation, and immune modulation culminating in HCC. However, it advances the original idea by integrating additional metabolic stress signals (ROS and α-dicarbonyl stress) that are supported by recent evidence, thereby explaining alternative pathways (such as RNF5 and RAGE signaling) that contribute to immune dysregulation. Furthermore, the revised concept leverages contemporary high-throughput and single-cell omics technologies to identify specific mRNA targets and to validate the mechanistic links, significantly enhancing the practical implementability and depth of the hypothesis.
